title: Wages held back (James 5:1–6)
hook: the wages you withheld cry out

segments.voice: Yesterday, if the Lord wills, and your line was a little while. Which good thing did you stop saving for someday? Day six hundred seventy-eight.

Sundown at the edge of a harvested field. The reapers have been cutting grain since morning, and now they wait for the day's pay. No savings account. No paycheck next Friday. The old law of Moses says why that pay can't wait: the worker is poor, and has set his heart on it. Tonight the owner says, come back next week. That's the scene behind today's passage. And James, who has been practical and plainspoken for four chapters, suddenly raises his voice.

In the King James Bible: "Go to now, ye rich men, weep and howl for your miseries that shall come upon you." It sounds like the old prophets, Amos or Isaiah, thundering against injustice. Then pictures of wealth rotting where it's stored: "Your riches are corrupted, and your garments are motheaten." The gold and silver, he says, have rusted, and the rust will be a witness against you. Hoarded things decay. Then the heart of it: "Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth." The wages themselves cry out. Money that should have been in a worker's hand has a voice. And it reaches God. Deuteronomy says to pay a poor laborer his wage on the same day, before the sun goes down, so that he doesn't cry to the Lord against you. James is drawing on that old command. And notice the title he uses for God. Lord of sabaoth. It isn't sabbath. It's a Hebrew word meaning armies, or hosts. The Lord of hosts. The commander of heaven's armies is listening to the cry of a farmhand who wasn't paid. Some churches teach from this passage that a fair wage, paid on time, isn't charity. It's justice.
screen: then, large: `KEPT BACK BY FRAUD, CRIETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pay someone promptly. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people whose work you depend on that you rarely see. The person who picks your fruit. Who cleans the office at night. Who delivers the packages. Who sews the clothes you're wearing. Picture one of them. Then think closer to home: do you owe anyone right now? An invoice, a babysitter, a friend who covered lunch, a bill you've let slide. Name it. Decide when you'll pay. If you pray, you can pray for workers who are waiting on wages. The bell holds the time.
Sabaoth. Hebrew for hosts, armies, the Lord of hosts: the title James uses when he says a worker's unpaid wages cry out and reach God's ears.
Your line: the wages cry out. Today, pay one thing you owe, a bill, a loan, a babysitter, sooner than you have to. Day six hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Some churches draw on James 5 and Deuteronomy 24 in their teaching on fair wages and workers' rights, and some congregations make a point of paying their own staff and contractors promptly and fairly.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rant against rich people.
what it means: withheld wages cry out, and God hears the unpaid worker.
what a scholar hears: the voice of the prophets, the law of Deuteronomy 24, and the Hebrew title 'Lord of hosts' kept in Greek letters.
